common_name: Rixford Dragon Fruit (Classic Purple-Fleshed Pitaya Breeding Parent)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring after all frost danger has passed, providing a sturdy post or trellis for the climbing cactus stems; in zone 9a grow in a large container that can be sheltered from freezes.

directions: Rixford is an older purple-fleshed dragon fruit selection long grown by California rare fruit enthusiasts, valued historically for its richly colored, deep red-purple flesh and good eating quality at a time when white-fleshed cultivars dominated commerce. It has gone on to become an important breeding parent in modern pitaya hybridizing, contributing its color and flavor to well-known newer selections such as Cosmic Charlie and Physical Graffiti. As a climbing epiphytic cactus, Rixford needs a sturdy post or trellis for support and very well-drained, sandy to loamy soil rather than regular irrigation. Flowers open for a single night and fruit set is more reliable with hand pollination after dusk, since self-fertility varies among individual plants of this older selection. Give it full sun and protect the succulent stems from any frost, since container culture with winter shelter is the most practical approach outside USDA zone 10-12.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Hylocereus and Selenicereus Varieties
Top Tropicals — Dragon Fruit Cultivar Notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dragon Fruit Production in Florida

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Dot is an older Florida dooryard selection grown today mostly by collectors and as breeding stock rather than for fresh-market fruit.

directions: Dot is a long-established Florida mango selection best known today as one of the parents, alongside Gary, of the popular dwarf condo-type mango Pina Colada, bred by Gary Zill in Boynton Beach. On its own merits it produces medium-sized fruit with yellow-orange blushed skin and smooth, fiberless, sweetly flavored flesh typical of early Florida dooryard mangoes rather than the more elaborate flavor profiles bred into recent introductions. Because mango wood has no frost tolerance at all, grow Dot in a large container that can be moved under cover during freezes, or reserve it for the warmest, most sheltered zone 10-11 planting site. Reduce irrigation as fruit approaches ripeness to concentrate sugars, and prune after harvest to maintain a manageable size and encourage the new growth that carries the following season's crop.
sources: Mango.org (National Mango Board) — Zill Mango Cultivar Descriptions
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mangifera indica Cultivar Records
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Home Landscape

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Gary is a Florida dooryard selection grown today chiefly for its role as breeding stock.

directions: Gary is a Florida mango selection remembered mainly as the pollen parent, alongside Dot, behind Pina Colada, the compact condo-type mango released by breeder Gary Zill around 2012. As a dooryard tree in its own right it produces medium fruit with fiberless, sweet flesh typical of the older Florida mango selections that underpin much of today's commercial breeding. Like all mango, it carries no frost tolerance whatsoever, so zone 9a-10a gardeners should grow Gary in a large container that can be sheltered during cold snaps, or in the warmest possible microclimate in zone 10-11. Give it full sun, well-drained fertile soil, and an annual post-harvest prune to keep a container specimen compact and productive.
sources: Mango.org (National Mango Board) — Zill Mango Cultivar Descriptions
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mangifera indica Cultivar Records
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Home Landscape

planting.note: Plant air-layered or grafted trees in spring once soil has warmed, in zone 9-10 set out March-May. Like other longans, Haew needs several weeks of cool, dry winter weather below roughly 60F to induce flowering, so keep irrigation minimal in winter. Protect young trees below 30F.

directions: Haew is one of Thailand's major commercial longan cultivars, grown alongside Edau and Chompoo and introduced to Florida trial plantings for side-by-side evaluation against the industry-standard Kohala, though Kohala remains more widely planted there. It bears large, thin-skinned fruit with a small seed and sweet, aromatic, translucent flesh that many growers rank among the best-flavored of the widely grown Thai longan selections. Like all longan, it needs a stretch of cool, relatively dry winter weather to set flower buds reliably, which makes zone 9 plantings with real winter chill more consistent bearers than frost-free zone 10-11 sites. Give it deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and expect a grafted or air-layered tree to begin bearing within four to five years.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — The Longan in Florida
University of Hawaii Cooperative Extension — Longan Production Guide
Rare Fruit Council International cultivar notes

subcategory: Brazilian Atlantic Forest myrtaceous berry tree

planting.note: Plant in spring in partial shade to full sun in fertile, moist, well-drained, acidic soil in zone 9-11; protect from hard frost below the upper 20s F.

directions: Cambuci is a small understory tree of the São Paulo region's Atlantic Forest, producing distinctive lantern- or acorn-shaped fruit with thin, fragile, pale yellow-green skin that bruises easily and does not ship well, which has kept it almost unknown outside Brazil. The pulp is intensely tart and aromatic rather than sweet, and is traditionally muddled into caipirinha-style cocktails, churned into sorbets and ice creams, or made into juice and liqueur rather than eaten plain. Unlike the smooth-skinned, trunk-clustered jaboticaba it resembles in family, cambuci fruits form singly or in small groups near the branch tips. Grow it in fertile, consistently moist, acidic soil with some shade, reflecting its forest-understory origin, and protect young plants from any hard freeze since cold tolerance is limited.
sources: Lorenzi, H. — Brazilian Fruits and Cultivated Exotics (2006)
Kew Science — Campomanesia phaea
Slow Food International Ark of Taste

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in lean, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; more tender than hardy wall germander, so site in zone 8-10 or a warm, sheltered microclimate.

directions: Teucrium lucidum is a compact, glossy-leaved Mediterranean subshrub closely related to hardy wall germander (Teucrium chamaedrys) but distinctly less cold-tolerant, and it is one of the two parent species behind the popular clipped-hedging hybrid Teucrium x lucidrys. Grown on its own, it forms a low, rounded mound of shiny, finely scalloped, aromatic leaves topped in summer with small two-lipped, rose-purple flowers that draw bees. Its tidy, naturally dense habit takes shearing well, making it suitable for low knot-garden edging in climates too mild to need its hybrid offspring's extra hardiness. Give it the same lean, sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil that all Mediterranean teucriums require, since wet or heavy ground quickly causes root and crown rot, and protect it through winter in anything colder than zone 8.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society plant records
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
Mediterranean flora reference literature

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; more heat- and drought-tolerant but less cold-hardy than Choisya ternata, so best in zone 8-10.

directions: Choisya arizonica is a smaller, more drought-adapted relative of the familiar Mexican orange blossom (Choisya ternata), native to dry rocky washes and slopes of Sonora, Mexico and adjacent southern Arizona rather than the moister highland forests its better-known cousin favors. Its trifoliate leaflets are narrower and finer-textured than those of C. ternata, giving the whole shrub a lighter, almost willowy look, while the fragrant white star-shaped flowers and citrus-scented foliage carry the same strong orange-blossom perfume. Breeders crossed it with C. ternata to create the widely grown hybrid Aztec Pearl, combining this species' narrow foliage with improved winter hardiness from its other parent. Grow Choisya arizonica in full sun on lean, fast-draining soil for the best heat and drought tolerance, and expect it to need more winter protection than C. ternata despite its desert origins, since it is adapted to dry heat rather than hard freezes.
sources: Southwestern desert native plant references
Royal Horticultural Society
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs propagated from cuttings in fall to allow root establishment through the rainy season, into lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; water only to establish, since summer irrigation on settled plants invites root rot.

directions: Ceanothus papillosus is a California native evergreen shrub named for the small, raised, wart-like glandular bumps that stud its narrow, resinous, dark-green leaves, a rough texture unlike the smoother foliage of most other ceanothus species. In spring it produces dense clusters of medium blue flowers that stand out sharply against this unusual leaf surface, and it has served as a parent species, alongside Ceanothus impressus, in breeding the popular deep-blue garden hybrid 'Concha'. Native to the dry chaparral and coastal-range soils of central and southern California, it is adapted to lean, nutrient-poor ground and shrugs off summer drought once established, but is quickly killed by root rot if given regular irrigation on settled soil. Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil, water only through the first season to establish roots, and then rely on winter rainfall for the life of the shrub.
sources: Calscape (California Native Plant Society)
Las Pilitas Nursery
California Flora Nursery

planting.note: Pot in a moisture-retentive terrestrial mix kept constantly damp; Phragmipedium longifolium flowers sequentially over an extended season and prefers bright, filtered light with intermediate temperatures year-round.

directions: Phragmipedium longifolium is a terrestrial slipper orchid found along stream banks and wet, rocky slopes in cloud forests from Costa Rica south through Colombia and into Peru. Rather than opening a single dramatic bloom like many slipper orchids, it flowers sequentially from the same inflorescence over many weeks, producing a succession of soft yellow-green blooms with twisted petals noticeably shorter than the extravagantly elongated petals of its relative Phragmipedium caudatum. It has long been valued as a breeding parent, passing its compact size and repeat-flowering habit on to classic hybrids such as 'Grande'. Keep the moisture-retentive terrestrial mix constantly damp and never allow the roots to dry out, and provide bright, filtered light with intermediate, cloud-forest-like temperatures for steady year-round growth and flowering.
sources: American Orchid Society
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew
Marie Selby Botanical Gardens
